verdict: AVOID for now — lend only to compliant, low-leverage dye/intermediate units with proven pass-through; skip the rest until air-consent and safety records clear.
title: Ahmedabad Chemicals, Dyes & Intermediates: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A dye or intermediate unit buys petro-derived feedstock, runs multi-step batch reactions in reactors, and sells drums of colour or chemical to textile, agrochem and export buyers.** Cash is made on conversion margin, not on the molecule: the spread between feedstock cost and selling price, minus power, steam and effluent treatment. Pricing power is thin and episodic — most units pass cost through with a lag, so a feedstock spike first hits the balance sheet, not the P&L. Working capital sits in inventory (feedstock plus in-process batches) and in receivables from textile and export buyers; capex is reactor trains, boilers and effluent plants, and the effluent plant is now the binding constraint, not the reactor. ## What has changed now
**The local shock is regulatory and safety, not demand.** Ahmedabad has issued closure notices to 19 factories in an air-pollution crackdown [1], and a chemical leak at a Naroli unit killed 2 and injured 7 [2] — note that source [2] is dated October 2024, so treat it as history, not fresh news. Nationally, chemicals output (NIC 20) is -0.5% YoY and -1.2% April-to-date [D], while bank credit to the sector runs +20.7% YoY against that falling output — a +21.9 pp gap [D]. **That gap is the real credit risk: money is chasing a shrinking pie.** Brent at $113/bbl sits above the $75–100 band [D], so feedstock and fuel costs stay elevated. Peer results are the counter-signal: Aarti Industries posted Q2 FY27 PAT up 60% to Rs. 169 crore on 30% volume growth [4], revenue up 75% to Rs. 3,668 crore [5], with record quarterly revenue and EBITDA [3][6]. **Scale players with long-term global supply agreements are winning; small converters are not.** Rating commentary flags elevated working-capital intensity that blocks capital in high-growth scenarios [8], and China dumping plus de-stocking pressure [7] — both undated, so verify currency. ## Where to grow
**Pursue mid-size specialty and intermediate makers with export or long-term supply contracts, and dye units selling to organised textile buyers.** These mirror the peer pattern of volume-led growth [4][5]. Avoid commodity dye converters with single-product dependence, units in Odhav or Vatva without a current consent-to-operate, and any borrower whose effluent or safety record is unclear. When a proposal lands, check the consent-to-operate and pollution-board status first; if it is expired or under notice, ask for the compliance plan and dated clearance before anything else. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle, not the fixed assets.** Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, quarterly GSTR-2B versus purchase register, and a covenant capping total outside liabilities to tangible net worth. Because feedstock is the swing cost, ask for the pass-through clause in customer contracts; if absent, ask for the last four quarters' gross margin to see who absorbed the spike. Collect from customer: current feedstock contract terms, effluent plant capacity, and insurance cover for the Naroli-type event. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch consent status, inventory days and receivable ageing together.** A closure notice [1] or a safety incident [2] stops production and cash at once. Rising inventory with flat sales means feedstock bought ahead of a price fall. Stretched receivables from textile buyers signal the downstream is stressed.

mismatch -> stop disbursement, reconcile before release
